summary: Peru grants visa-free entry of up to 90 days (capped at 183 days in any 365-day period) to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas, records arrivals digitally with no paper entry form, and lets Chinese and Indian citizens who hold a valid US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa enter without a Peruvian visa.

passportValidity.text: Peru expects your passport to be valid for at least 6 months on the date of entry — airlines routinely enforce this before boarding.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: Not checked at the border for most arrivals, but the Peruvian health ministry strongly recommends (and jungle regions expect) yellow fever vaccination for travel to the Amazon below about 2,300 m — Iquitos, Puerto Maldonado, Tarapoto and jungle lodges. It is not needed for Lima, Cusco, the Sacred Valley or Machu Picchu.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement, but medical coverage is strongly recommended — private clinics expect payment up front, and altitude-related evacuations from the Andes are expensive.

onwardTicket.text: Not a formal legal requirement, but airlines and immigration officers frequently ask for proof of onward or return travel. Carry a booking that leaves Peru within your permitted stay.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is set, but officers may ask about your means of support, itinerary and accommodation when deciding how many days to grant.

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments over USD 10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure; carrying more than USD 30,000 in cash is prohibited.

source.name: SUNAT — Peruvian customs and tax authority

notes: There is no paper entry form. The old Andean Migration Card (TAM) is digital and generated automatically at passport control; note the number of days written or stamped, as that is your permitted stay.
Personal electronics such as a laptop and phone enter duty-free; strict rules protect archaeological artefacts — exporting antiques or pre-Columbian items is a crime.
Coca leaves and coca tea are legal in Peru but illegal to take into most other countries, including the US and the EU.

payments.text: Cards are widely accepted in Lima, Cusco and Arequipa hotels, restaurants and shops, but cash rules in markets, small towns, taxis and the countryside. Carry soles in small notes — change for 100-sol bills is scarce — and use ATMs inside banks or malls.

safety.text: Most visits to Peru's tourist circuit are trouble-free, but petty theft is common in Lima and Cusco, express kidnappings via unofficial taxis occur, and some border and remote coca-growing regions (the VRAEM) should be avoided. Use registered taxis or ride-hailing apps and keep valuables out of sight.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Peru travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September is the dry season in the Andes — the best window for Cusco, Machu Picchu and trekking (book the Inca Trail months ahead); Lima's coast is gray then but pleasant December–March.

idp.text: Peru is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Peru is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Peru yet.

tips.text: Cusco sits at 3,400 m. Plan a light first day, hydrate, and consider acclimatising in the lower Sacred Valley (2,800 m) before the city or any trek. Altitude sickness can hit anyone regardless of fitness.
Machu Picchu entry tickets are limited, timed and sold out weeks ahead in high season (June–August). Buy them and Inca Trail permits well in advance through official channels only.

Never hail unmarked street taxis in Lima. Use ride-hailing apps or hotel-arranged, registered taxis. Express kidnappings and robberies via informal taxis are the most common serious crime against visitors.
Tap water is not safe to drink anywhere in Peru. Stick to bottled, boiled or filtered water, including for brushing teeth in jungle areas.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Peru visa-free for tourism. Border officers typically grant up to 90 days per entry, with total stays capped at 183 days in any 365-day period. There is no fee and no paper form; entry is recorded digitally.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Peru as a tourist?
faq.answer: Visa-exempt visitors get up to 90 days per entry at the officer's discretion, within a hard cap of 183 days in any 365-day period. You can request an extension up to that cap through Migraciones' online Agencia Digital before your granted days run out.

faq.question: Do Chinese or Indian citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: Normally yes — a consular tourist visa. However, Chinese and Indian citizens holding a valid US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa (or permanent residence in those places) can enter Peru without a Peruvian visa for tourism or business, for up to 180 days. Confirm current rules with a Peruvian consulate before booking.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccine for Machu Picchu or the Amazon?
faq.answer: Not for Machu Picchu, Cusco or Lima. These are outside the risk zone. Vaccination is strongly recommended if you will visit the Amazon below about 2,300 m (Iquitos, Puerto Maldonado, Manu, Tambopata); get the shot at least 10 days before travel.

faq.question: Do I need to fill in an entry form (TAM) for Peru?
faq.answer: No. The old paper Andean Migration Card (TAM) was replaced by a digital record created automatically at passport control. There is nothing to fill in before travel — just check how many days the officer grants you, as that is your permitted stay.
